sections.title: P8-Q1 — registrar vs nested ServiceProvider
sections.text:
**Query:** Answer in prose, no tables. In PHP Laravel 11/12 package development,
why should an internal composition helper that only binds services into the
container NOT extend Illuminate\Support\ServiceProvider? Contrast nested
ServiceProvider subclasses versus a small registrar/compiler-pass style object
with register(Application $app): void. How can a nested provider be accidentally
auto-discovered via extra.laravel.providers or package auto-discovery? How do
Symfony compiler passes compile contributions before the container is frozen,
and why is a compiler pass not itself a bundle? Cite Laravel packages docs,
Laravel service container docs, Symfony compiler passes / dependency injection
compilation. Name primary-source URLs.

**Status:** success

An internal composition helper should be a plain object when its only job is
to add bindings. Extending ServiceProvider advertises a framework lifecycle
participant that Laravel may discover, instantiate, defer, boot and cache —
not a reusable unit of container composition.

Laravel service providers are package bootstrap components: register() adds
bindings; boot() runs after other providers are registered. A package provider
also owns publishes, routes, views, migrations and commands. A registrar has a
smaller contract: `register(Application $app): void`. The public package
provider remains the single Laravel entry point. The registrar has no
independent discovery, boot, deferral or provider-cache semantics and can be
unit-tested by passing an application instance.

A nested `$this->app->register(InternalProvider::class)` works mechanically
but makes internal modules look like independently valid providers. Maintainers
later add boot(), DeferrableProvider or publishing. The class can leak into
`extra.laravel.providers`, `bootstrap/providers.php`, or a copied README.
Package discovery then treats it as a top-level entry; duplicated side effects
and surprising binding order follow. Safe posture: expose exactly the public
package provider in Composer auto-discovery.

If a registrar later needs post-registration work, do not add a casual boot()
look-alike. Model two narrow phases — `register` and `boot` — and have the one
public provider invoke them from its own register() and boot().

Symfony first collects definitions, then runs compiler passes on
ContainerBuilder, then dumps the compiled container. A compiler pass is a
build-time transformation, not a bundle. A bundle is the modular integration
unit and may register passes from build(). Analogies: Symfony bundle ≈ Laravel
package plus its public provider; compiler pass ≈ internal registrar for
modular contributions. Not equivalent mechanically: Laravel providers execute
against the runtime container during bootstrap.

Primary sources: https://laravel.com/docs/12.x/providers ·
https://laravel.com/docs/12.x/packages ·
https://symfony.com/doc/current/components/dependency_injection/workflow.html

[листинг сокращён: BillingRegistrar и PackageServiceProvider]

sections.title: P8-Q2 — when a composition module is justified
sections.text:
**Query:** Answer in prose, no tables. What makes a composition module
justified versus splitting a DI container registration into a class per two
bindings? Cite Mark Seemann Composition Root, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection
service registration grouping, and Fowler bounded context / module cohesion.
When should optional integration wiring (class_exists / interface_exists of a
neighboring package) live in its own registrar that can be omitted, versus
remaining in the main bootstrap? Name primary-source URLs.

**Status:** success

A composition module is justified when it expresses a real architectural unit
of wiring: a feature, adapter family, bounded context, runtime mode, or
independently optional integration. It is not justified because two
registrations happen to be adjacent. “One class per two bindings” turns the
Composition Root into a directory of fragments with no ownership boundary.

Seemann: an application should have a preferably unique Composition Root near
its entry point; application code should not depend on the container. Splitting
the root into helpers is compatible only if the entry-point bootstrap remains
the readable top-level manifest of the object graph.

The practical test: what changes together, is owned together, and can be
enabled, replaced or tested together? Microsoft’s convention is a single
`Add{GroupName}` method that registers the services required for a feature.
The significant word is group: a feature-level contract, not an arbitrary
batch size.

Fowler’s bounded context: registrations belong together when they support one
reason to change. Do not invent tiny pseudo-modules where no distinct model,
ownership or change boundary exists.

Optional neighboring-package wiring belongs in its own omittable registrar
when the neighbor is genuinely optional at install or deployment time and the
base package must remain usable without it. Keep probing at the outer
composition boundary; domain code depends on its own port. If the neighbor is
actually mandatory, `class_exists()` hides a broken installation — fail fast
through Composer constraints and configuration validation instead.

Primary sources: https://blog.ploeh.dk/2011/07/28/CompositionRoot/ ·
https://blog.ploeh.dk/2019/06/17/composition-root-location/ ·
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/dependency-injection/service-registration ·
https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BoundedContext.html

sections.title: P8-Q3 — boot APIs without ServiceProvider
sections.text:
**Query:** Answer in prose, no tables. Laravel 11/12: how can a class that does
NOT extend ServiceProvider register Artisan commands, load route files, alias
middleware, and subscribe to events during application boot? Show the
Application or Kernel APIs a registrar can call from boot(Application $app).
Contrast with $this->commands() and $this->loadRoutesFrom() which require a
ServiceProvider. Cite Laravel console kernel, routing, events docs or
framework source. Name primary-source URLs.

**Status:** success

A class does not need to extend ServiceProvider. Treat it as a boot-time
registrar: resolve framework services from Application and call their public
APIs. `$this->commands()` and `$this->loadRoutesFrom()` belong to
Illuminate\Support\ServiceProvider.

Commands: resolve `Illuminate\Contracts\Console\Kernel` and call
`registerCommand` on an instance, or the concrete kernel’s `addCommands`.
Laravel’s ApplicationBuilder::withCommands() ultimately defers to the console
kernel. `Artisan::starting` plus `resolveCommands` is the same path the
provider helper uses.

HTTP routes: resolve `Illuminate\Routing\Router` and `group($path)`. Provider
`loadRoutesFrom()` skips the file when routes are cached. A naked
`Router::group($file)` does not. A registrar that requires a route file must
guard with `$app->routesAreCached()`.

Middleware aliases: `$router->aliasMiddleware($name, $class)`. Register
aliases before loading route files that use them.

Events: `Illuminate\Contracts\Events\Dispatcher::listen` or `subscribe`.
Do not capture a scoped service in a long-lived listener closure; resolve
per event.

`publishes()` and `mergeConfigFrom()` stay on the Laravel provider: they are
provider helpers, not Application APIs.

Primary sources: https://laravel.com/docs/12.x/events ·
https://api.laravel.com/docs/12.x/doc-index.html
